def: A researcher who has successfully completed the necessary ethics, governance, and training requirements to receive NSHD data. Approval is granted on a per-project basis and is tied to a specific data access request submitted via Skylark. Data may only be used by the named approved researchers for the stated project purpose.

A Showcase field attribute indicating whether multiple measurements were taken per participant per visit. All NSHD fields show No. Where Array is Yes, the data will contain more than one value per participant per sweep, which affects how the data is structured in a request.

Files attached to a variable on the NSHD metadata page providing supporting documentation. There are two types: Link to the the Questionnaires page on the website — giving access to the original survey instrument showing the exact question wording, response options, and respondent type; and Documents — additional technical files such as measurement guides, topic documentation, or derivation specifications available for download. Not all variables have associated documents beyond the questionnaire link.

The loss of study members from the cohort over time, whether through death, withdrawal, or loss of contact. Attrition is common in long-running studies and is one reason sample sizes shrink in later sweeps compared to earlier ones.

A collection of variables selected by a researcher in preparation for a data access request. In OWL, variables can be added to the basket from any results table — Search Data Dictionary, Browse by Category, Popular Variables or Longitudinal search. The basket page summarises all selected variables before submission.
A study design that follows the same group of people from birth onward, rather than recruiting participants at a later age or following different people at each time point.

A section of OWL that organises variables into a hierarchical tree of categories and subcategories, allowing users to navigate by topic area rather than searching by name. Each category page lists the variables it contains with their names, Field IDs, and labels. A variable can belong to more than one category.

An internal reference on the NSHD metadata page that links a variable to a specific dataset (library file). Useful to see which variables were also in the dataset as the variable of interest. Some datasets are grouped by type of data and some by the questionnaire instrument

A variable type where each response is one of a fixed set of coded categories, such as Yes/No or a 5-point rating scale, rather than a measured numeric value. On the NSHD Showcase, the Value type attribute distinguishes Categorical (single) — one response per participant per sweep — from Categorical (multiple), where more than one option may be selected. Contrast with Continuous.

The classification and grouping of a variable by topic domain. A variable can belong to more than one category on the NSHD metadata page — for example, a body size measure may appear under both a legacy Anthropometry category and a current Body size measures subcategory. The NSHD Showcase shows one primary category with its full hierarchical parent and child path.

The hierarchical tree structure of categorising variables, in which broad top-level categories (such as Clinical data) contain subcategories (such as Cognitive function), which in turn contain the individual variables. The breadcrumb path shown at the top of each category page reflects a variable's position in this tree.

The group of individuals followed by the study, in this case everyone born in England, Scotland, and Wales during one week of March 1946. A birth cohort study follows the same people from birth, distinguishing it from studies that recruit at a later age.

The specialised metadata and data sharing platform created by NSHD staff to request variables for a scientific proposal. Condor holds the similar variable-level metadata as OWL — questionnaire provenance, longitudinal linkage, category placement, and distribution summaries — but is accessible only to authorised staff and bonafide researchers. Access is subject to registration and internal approval.

A variable type representing a numeric measured value, such as height, weight, or blood pressure, rather than a fixed set of coded categories. Continuous variables are summarised on the OWL variable metadata page using statistics such as the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and deciles. Contrast with Categorical.

A secure, controlled and trusted research environment (TRE) in which NSHD data must be accessed and analysed. The DSH prevents data from being downloaded to personal or institutional devices and ensures that only approved researchers can view the data, only for their approved project.

A legally binding agreement between the NSHD and a researchers institution governing the conditions under which NSHD data may be accessed, stored, used, and shared. Data sharing agreements specify permitted uses, security requirements, and obligations around publication and data destruction. A signed agreement is typically required before data is released via the UCL Data Safe Haven (DSH).

One of nine values that divide an ordered continuous distribution into ten equal groups. Decile 1 is the value below which 10% of observations fall; Decile 9 is the value below which 90% fall. Deciles are shown in the distribution panel of the OWL variable metadata page for continuous variables, alongside the minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, and series size.

A field on the NSHD metadata page indicating whether a variable was collected directly or calculated. 0 means the variable was directly measured or recorded during data collection. 1 means it is a derived variable, calculated from one or more other variables.

A variable calculated from one or more raw measurements rather than collected directly, for example Body Mass Index derived from separately measured height and weight, or a summary score combining several questionnaire items.

Rules applied to publicly displayed data to protect participant confidentiality. On OWL and Condor, two controls are applied: response categories with fewer than 10 observations are suppressed from display; and for continuous variables, values below the 5th percentile and above the 95th percentile are excluded from plots and summary statistics. The series size shown in distribution panels reflects only the observations remaining after these controls are applied.

A numeric identifier that links a variable in the OWL to its entry on the NSHD Showcase. Variables sharing the same Field ID and identical question text and coding are grouped together on a single Showcase page, with each sweep shown as a separate instance.

The data collection instrument a variable was collected from, for example: postal questionnaire, nurse schedule, home visit, CAPI interview, or medical examination. Together with Question and Year, this tells you exactly where to find the original question in the source instrument.

A visual and tabular summary of how values are spread across study members for a variable. For categorical variables this takes the form of a bar chart and count table; for continuous variables a histogram and summary statistics (minimum, deciles, maximum, mean, standard deviation). Disclosure controls apply: response categories with fewer than 10 observations are suppressed, and the bottom and top 5% of continuous distributions are excluded from display.
A neuroimaging sub-study of a subset of NSHD study members, collected in three phases (Insight46 Phase 3 is still on-going).

On the NSHD Showcase, each sweep at which a field was collected is shown as a separate instance, labelled with its time period — for example, Instance 26: 2006–2010. Variables are only grouped into a multi-instance field where the question text and coding are identical across all sweeps; where they differ, each sweep appears as its own Showcase entry.

The total number of individual data points available across all sweeps for a Showcase field. For multi-sweep fields this exceeds the participant count — for example, if 2,400 participants each have data at 4 time points, item count would be approximately 9,600.
A Showcase field attribute indicating the nature of the data. Data means the field contains actual collected measurements. Other types may indicate derived or administrative fields.

A field on the NSHD metadata page that indicates whether a more recent or corrected version of a variable exists. NA means the variable is current. Always check this field before including a variable in a data request — if a later version exists, use that instead.

A category from an older version of category classification system, retained for reference but superseded by current categories. Legacy categories are shown with a grey badge in the Categories tab of the OWL variable metadata page and are not linked to a live category page. These are not shown on the Showcase as only one catergory per variable is allowed on the Showcase

An OWL-specific grouping of collection years into broad age bands (for example Age 46–55 or Age 56–65), used to summarise variable coverage across the study’s history on the Data Coverage page. Life stage bands are a presentational grouping only and are not a field present in the underlying data dictionary.

A section on the Condor variable metadata page listing every variable connected to the current one for longitudinal or conceptual comparison, regardless of whether question text or coding stayed identical across sweeps. Broader than Truly Longitudinal, which only includes the strict same-Field-ID subset.

On the OWL metadata page, variables that have been deliberately associated with the current variable to support longitudinal or conceptual comparison. Linkage is flexible — variables can be connected because they measure the same construct at another sweep, even if question wording or coding changed, or because they form part of the same scale or instrument. This is broader than the NSHD Showcase grouping, which only links variables with strictly identical question text and coding.

Describes data collected repeatedly over time from the same individuals, allowing change to be tracked within a person rather than only compared across different people at a single point. The NSHD is a longitudinal study by design. See also: Birth cohort study, Sweep, Truly Longitudinal, Linked & Longitudinal (Condor).

A dedicated OWL page listing every Field ID collected with identical question text and coding across two or more sweeps — true longitudinal measures — with a sweep-by-sweep trajectory chart and statistics table for each one. Reachable directly from any variable's own metadata page via a 'View all in Longitudinal Search' link. See also: Truly Longitudinal.

The arithmetic average of a continuous variable, calculated by summing all values and dividing by the number of observations. Shown in the distribution panel of the OWL variable metadata page. The mean is calculated after disclosure controls are applied — missing values and values outside the 5th–95th percentile range are excluded — so it reflects the distribution of plotted values only.

The ongoing initiative to clean, document, and enhance NSHD variable metadata, making it available on OWL, Condor and the NSHD Showcase. Only variables processed through this project are currently visible on those two platforms — the remainder of the NSHD’s 35,000+ variables are available on Condor only, pending processing.

A Showcase Field ID for which more than one distinct collection year is on record, meaning the field was genuinely collected at more than one time point with identical question text and coding. These are the fields the NSHD Showcase groups together as multiple Instances. Contrast with Single-sweep Field ID.

Free-text contextual information attached to a variable on the NSHD metadata page. May include measurement conditions, known caveats about the data, recoding details, or quality notes specific to this variable — for example, whether a height measurement was taken with or without shoes. This information is not available on the NSHD Showcase.

On the NSHD Showcase, the Notes section primarily lists the sweep-specific NSHD variable names and labels covered by a multi-instance field — for example, listing ghi09, ghi14x, ghi22x for a self-rated health field collected at different ages. Useful for cross-referencing Showcase instance numbers back to specific NSHD variable names.

National Survey of Health and Development — the formal name for the 1946 birth cohort study that OWL, the NSHD Showcase, and Condor all provide access to. Also referred to simply as ‘the 1946 cohort’ or ‘the study’ throughout OWL’s documentation.

A publicly accessible data catalogue for the NSHD, modelled on the UK Biobank Showcase. The Showcase groups variables that share the same Field ID and identical question text and coding onto a single page, with each sweep presented as a separate instance. It provides participant counts, item counts, value types, and distribution summaries, and is accessed via the Field ID link in OWL search results or variable metadata pages.

The Online Wellbeing and Lifecourse Resource — the public-facing platform for exploring NSHD variable metadata and documentation. OWL allows users to search for variables using multiple methods whilst giving users access to the original questionnaires and documentation. Researchers can view metadata and distribution summaries, and build a basket of variables for a data access request.

A category that contains subcategories. Navigating to a parent category page may show no variables — the variables sit in its child subcategories (some parent categories may have variables). The category tree breadcrumb helps identify where in the hierarchy a category sits.

On the NSHD Showcase, the number of unique study members who have at least one data point for a field. For multi-sweep fields, this is the count of distinct individuals across all time points combined, not per sweep.

A curated list of frequently requested or commonly used NSHD variables, available as a starting point for researchers new to the dataset. Variables can be added to the basket directly from the Popular Variables page.

The specific question number within the collection form that generated a variable, for example 96(a). Together with Form and Year on the NSHD metadata page, this allows you to locate the exact question in the original questionnaire.

A field on the NSHD metadata page stating why a variable is publicly visible in the OWL. Not applicable if no specific reason is recorded. Most variables are public by default; this field is populated only where a specific justification has been noted.

A field on the NSHD metadata page explaining why a variable is marked as sensitive — for example due to low cell counts or nature of the variable. Not applicable if the variable is not sensitive. See also: Sensitive.

Some variables are not publicly displayed in full due to data sensitivity, identifiability, or governance restrictions. If you believe you need access to a restricted variable for a project, contact the NSHD data access team directly.

The main search interface in OWL, allowing users to search across all NSHD variable names and labels by keyword. Results are displayed in a table with variable name, Field ID, and label, and variables can be added to the basket or clicked through to their full metadata page.

A field on the NSHD metadata page indicating whether a variable has access restrictions. 0 means publicly visible in the OWL. 1 means restricted — the variable may not be fully displayed and may require additional data access permissions to include in a request. See also: Restricted variable.

The number of observations included in a frequency distribution after disclosure controls have been applied and missing values excluded. For continuous variables, this excludes missing values and values outside the 5th–95th percentile range. For categorical variables, it excludes missing values and suppressed categories with fewer than 10 observations. Series size will therefore typically be smaller than the total number of study members with data for that variable.
A Showcase field attribute indicating whether data is available for both sexes or is specific to one sex. For example, variables from the Women's Health questionnaires are female-only.

A Showcase Field ID collected at only one distinct time point, with no repeat sweep sharing the same question text and coding. Shown as its own single instance on the NSHD Showcase. Contrast with Multi-sweep Field ID.

The NSHD data access platform through which researchers submit formal requests for NSHD data. Once a basket of variables has been formally saved on Condor, a data access request is submitted via Skylark. Skylark handles the full data request workflow — from application submission through ethics and governance review to data release.

A measure of the spread or variability of a continuous variable, expressed in the same units as the variable itself. A low standard deviation means values cluster closely around the mean; a high one means they are more spread out. Shown in the distribution panel of the OWL/Condor variable metadata page, calculated after disclosure controls are applied.

A Showcase field attribute indicating whether a variable comes from the main NSHD cohort or a sub-study. Primary means core cohort data collected from the main study sample. Secondary indicates sub-study or derived data, for example from Insight 46.
The everyday term for an individual participant in the NSHD cohort, used throughout OWL’s documentation and questionnaires.

A child category within category tree hierarchy, sitting beneath a broader parent category. For example, Body size measures is a subcategory of Clinical data. In OWL and Condor, a variable can belong to more than one subcategory as it can also belong to a legacy category.

One of four increasingly specific classification fields (Subtopic 1 through Subtopic 4) attached to each variable in the data dictionary, sitting beneath Topic in the classification hierarchy. Not every variable is classified to all four levels.

A single round of data collection from study members at a particular age or year. For example, the 1989 sweep collected data when study members were 43. The NSHD has had 36 sweeps spanning birth to age 76–77, each with its own questionnaire and set of variables.

The top-level classification field in the underlying data dictionary, shown as a column in Search Data Dictionary and Browse by Category results. Each variable’s Topic value feeds directly into Browse by Category’s top-level folders. See also: Category tree, Category membership.

A tab on the OWL variable metadata page listing only those variables that share the same Field ID with strictly identical question text and coding across sweeps — the same strict grouping used by the NSHD Showcase. Contrast with Linked & Longitudinal (Condor), which is broader and includes variables connected for any reason, even where wording or coding changed.

The UK Longitudinal Linkage Collaboration, a national initiative connecting data across multiple UK longitudinal cohort studies. Variables in the NSHD data dictionary that have been mapped to a UKLLC-recognised dataset show this in the ‘UKLLC Dataset Name(s)’ column in the data dictionary.

The unit of measurement for continuous variables on the NSHD metadata page, for example cm, kg, or mmHg. Shows Not applicable for categorical variables where responses are coded categories rather than measured quantities.

The coded values for a categorical variable and what each code means — for example, 1 = Excellent, 2 = Very good, 3 = Good. Special system codes such as 77 (No questionnaire) or 99 (Unknown) are also listed. For continuous variables, value labels typically represent missing data codes rather than substantive responses and are excluded from plots and statistics.

A Showcase field attribute that is the definitive statement of a variable's data type. Categorical (single) means one coded response per participant per sweep. Categorical (multiple) means more than one response may be selected. Continuous means a numeric measured value such as height or blood pressure.
The plain-English description of what a variable measures, paired with its coded variable name in the data dictionary.

The short, coded identifier used in the dataset, e.g. WIC82, usually combining an abbreviation with the sweep year. Variable names are often reused with different suffixes across sweeps to show the same question asked repeatedly over time.

The average of the squared differences from the mean, giving a measure of how spread out the values of a continuous variable are. Variance is the square of the standard deviation. Shown in the distribution panel of the OWL variable metadata page, calculated after disclosure controls are applied.

The term used specifically for each round of the three Covid sub-studies (Covid wave 1, 2, and 3), as distinct from the general term Sweep used for the main NSHD data collection rounds. Note that all three Covid waves can share the same broad Year of collection label — for example 2020 — even though they were collected as separate rounds months apart.

The year or year range in which a variable was collected ro collected up to, corresponding to a specific study sweep — for example 2006–10. Together with Form and Question on the NSHD metadata page, Year tells you exactly when the data was collected and allows you to find the original instrument.
